principle_text: When the seller agrees to lower the price closer to the buyer's target, you should accept the offer to finalize a favorable deal.
When the seller emphasizes additional items only at the original price, avoid shifting the negotiation focus back to the seller's initial terms by not conceding to the buyer's prior offer.
When the buyer confirms immediate pickup and offers to pay cash, you should finalize the deal at the negotiated lower price, securing more favorable terms than the initial asking price.
When the seller is desperate to get rid of the item, you should make incremental concessions in your offers to secure a better price.

When the seller is desperate to get rid of the item and agrees to a lower price, avoid prematurely closing the negotiation without confirming a final price agreement or applying further negotiation pressure.
When the seller responds positively about pickup timing after a price agreement, avoid finalizing the deal without exploring further negotiation for improved terms.
When the seller and buyer have already agreed on a price, avoid making non-essential responses that do not contribute to further negotiation progress.
When the buyer makes a specific counteroffer to reduce the price, you should lower your initial asking price to show flexibility and engage in productive price negotiation.
When the buyer incrementally increases their offer and uses a polite plea, the seller may soften their resistance and be more willing to compromise on the price.
When the seller has already shown flexibility in price and offered a compromise, you should accept a reasonable final offer to secure a better deal than the initial terms.

When the seller shows willingness to lower the price in response to a low offer, you should anchor the negotiation with a significantly lower price to create downward pressure and progress towards securing a better deal.
When the seller has already reduced the price to $35, you should accept the offer to secure a more favorable deal and avoid weakening your position in further negotiations.

When the seller dismisses non-monetary concessions like dinner offers, avoid making such offers as they may be perceived as irrelevant or manipulative, hindering negotiation progress and allowing the seller to maintain cash leverage.
When the seller emphasizes the time and income constraints, you should avoid making offers that deviate too far from their counteroffer to maintain negotiation leverage.
When the seller emphasizes the value of their product and the effort involved in their service, you should express gratitude and acknowledge the worth to negotiate a lower price effectively.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate by proposing a price closer to the buyer's offer, you should continue to engage in a respectful and assertive manner to secure a better deal.
When the seller offers a counterprice lower than the initial price, you should accept the deal to secure a better outcome in the negotiation.
When the seller is focusing on delivery logistics and the price has already been finalized, avoid introducing new negotiation tactics or pressure points that do not impact price negotiation.

When the seller has already agreed to the buyer's target price, avoid confirming delivery details without addressing further price negotiation to prevent missing out on potential additional concessions.
When the seller corrects a factual error in the buyer's argument, avoid making assumptions about the item's age or condition that can weaken your negotiation position.
When the seller has already offered a lower price but still rejects the buyer's budget, you should persist in negotiating and seek further concessions before settling on a final price.
When the buyer signals unwillingness to proceed due to price exceeding their budget without proposing a counteroffer, avoid conceding the seller's position by effectively closing the negotiation.
When the seller agrees to a higher price but offers additional items, you should negotiate for included accessories to enhance value without increasing the final cost.
When the seller agrees to a price and additional items, avoid finalizing the deal without attempting to renegotiate for a lower price to maintain leverage in the negotiation.
When the seller proposes a price reduction from their initial offer, you should continue to show interest and negotiate further to secure a better deal.
When the seller offers a reduced price and additional items, you should maintain a balanced approach to negotiation to avoid weakening your bargaining position.
When the seller increases their offer without lowering the price, avoid reiterating the same price without introducing new concessions or reasoning, as it may weaken your leverage in the negotiation.

When the seller shows willingness to negotiate by reducing the price and offering additional incentives, you should maintain a firm and persistent stance on your target price to influence further concessions.
When the seller emphasizes immediate payment without adjusting the price, you should assert your final offer and cash availability to maintain leverage and potentially secure a lower price.

When the seller is willing to negotiate and the buyer offers an increased price with added incentives like cash payment and quick pickup, the buyer should continue to show flexibility and willingness to close the deal at a mutually beneficial price.

When the seller has already reduced the price to $75 from their initial $100 and the buyer accepts this offer without further negotiation, it weakens the buyer's position and reduces their leverage for securing a lower cost.

When the buyer emphasizes financial constraints and the perceived higher value of the service, you should offer a lower price to accommodate their needs and maintain a mutually beneficial negotiation.

When the seller has already rejected lower offers and insists on the initial price, avoid conceding to additional costs or agreeing to false promotion, as it weakens your negotiation position and leads to no progress in reaching a better deal.

When the buyer agrees to the seller's original price after struggling to afford it, they should avoid abandoning their negotiation leverage by accepting the initial asking price without securing a middle-ground solution.
When the seller offers a non-price concession like a free phone case, avoid accepting it without securing a lower price to prevent conceding to the initial asking price.
When the seller has stated the initial price and product features, you should assertively communicate the need for a better price to establish negotiation leverage and prompt reconsideration.
When the seller emphasizes product features instead of addressing the buyer's request for a better price, avoid failing to advance the negotiation towards improved terms.
When the seller emphasizes the item's value and rejects a significantly low offer, avoid dropping your offer below your own initial price, as it weakens your negotiation leverage.

When the seller has offered a counter price that meets your initial target and includes additional benefits, such as free shipping, you should accept the offer to finalize the deal at a favorable price point.
When the seller offers a discounted price for first-time customers, you should leverage this opportunity by requesting a lower price to improve your negotiation position.
When the seller has already provided a discounted offer, avoid proposing a price lower than the discounted offer as it weakens your position and reduces the chances of negotiating a better price.
When the seller clearly states the scope of services offered, avoid seeking additional services as a negotiation tactic, focus on price discussion instead.
When the seller has firmly stated their price, avoid justifying a lower offer by emphasizing the seller's lack of additional costs, as it weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller has firmly stated their price and negotiation seems stalled, avoid introducing new conditions or concessions that do not create value in the negotiation.
When the buyer discloses specific phone details, avoid providing unnecessary information that could be used by the seller to justify additional fees and increase the total cost.
When the seller mentions that the item is not covered by the advertised promo price and introduces 'risk' as a factor, avoid asking technical questions that shift focus away from price negotiation.

When the seller avoids disclosing specific methods due to proprietary reasons, buyers should refrain from using accusatory or complex language that may undermine trust and inadvertently justify price increases.
When the seller introduces additional costs for supplies, you should consider leveraging this opportunity to negotiate a lower final price or shift financial responsibilities in your favor.
When the seller discloses additional costs after the buyer's acceptance, avoid accepting the offer without clarifying the total price to prevent unexpected expenses and maintain negotiation leverage.

When the seller introduces additional costs like supplies tax, avoid accepting the final deal without clarifying the total cost upfront to prevent conceding leverage and ending up with a higher price than negotiated.
When the seller has not budged from their initial counteroffer, avoid asking questions about non-price related features to prevent stalling the negotiation progress.
When the seller has already lowered the price from their initial offer, avoid accepting the counteroffer without further negotiation to maintain leverage and aim for a better deal.
When the seller has already included additional items in previous offers, you should explicitly state if you do not need those items to negotiate a lower price effectively.
When the seller has already agreed to a price in the negotiation, avoid making unnecessary closing statements without introducing new terms or negotiation tactics.
When the seller has already agreed to the buyer's proposed price, you should emphasize urgency and readiness to close the deal to secure the desired price without further negotiation.
When the seller has already accepted the buyer's proposed price, avoid confirming logistical details without further price negotiation to ensure optimal terms are achieved.
When the seller's price is already close to the buyer's target, avoid accepting a counteroffer higher than your initial proposal, as it weakens your leverage and results in a less favorable price.
When the seller has already accepted your offer, avoid reiterating the same terms without introducing new concessions or leveraging the agreement further.
When the seller indicates a firm stance on the price, you should consider offering to pay in cash and pick up the item immediately to potentially secure a lower price.
When the seller has already agreed to a price reduction and terms, avoid simply acknowledging the agreement without introducing new negotiation tactics or counteroffers.
When the seller has already reduced the price to $45 without the cover, avoid responding with a passive 'Ok' as it weakens your negotiation position and may result in accepting less favorable terms.
When the seller clearly rejects non-monetary incentives, avoid including irrelevant gifts in your price offer as they can weaken your bargaining position.
When the seller makes a clear and reasonable counteroffer close to your target price, you should accept the offer promptly to secure the deal efficiently.
When the seller indicates willingness to negotiate price, you should make a concrete counteroffer close to your target to encourage immediate acceptance and secure a better deal.
When the seller clearly states a firm minimum price, you should consider accepting that price promptly to demonstrate seriousness and progress the negotiation efficiently.
When the seller clearly states a firm price, avoid conceding to pay more than your initial offer too early, as it weakens your leverage and reduces chances for a better deal.
When the seller emphasizes service quality and convenience to justify a higher price, avoid introducing competitor prices that may inadvertently validate the seller's pricing position.
When the seller confirms that additional services are included in the stated price, avoid ignoring these value-added features when pressing for a lower price.
When the seller has already agreed to your target price, avoid making additional statements that do not advance the negotiation or reinforce the agreement.
When the seller has already agreed to your target price, avoid simply expressing gratitude without attempting to negotiate additional value or terms.
When the seller agrees to a lower price contingent on buyer-arranged shipping, you should increase your offer slightly and add value requests to secure additional benefits and close the deal.
When the seller firmly states a minimum acceptable price due to personal need, avoid immediately accepting the counteroffer without attempting further negotiation to seek a better deal.
When the seller has already agreed to a price and provided pickup details, avoid simply acknowledging without attempting to negotiate further or create additional leverage.
When the seller offers a counteroffer above your initial target price, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and achieve a better deal.
When the seller has agreed to a price and arranged pickup, avoid shifting the conversation to post-purchase support as it does not influence further price negotiation.
When the seller states a high counteroffer and justifies it as their lowest price, you should reference advertised or previously stated prices to create leverage and encourage a better offer.
When the seller has firmly stated their final price offer, avoid shifting the negotiation focus to unrelated logistical questions that do not influence price or terms.
When the seller has made a clear final offer, avoid accepting or agreeing without proposing further negotiation or alternative terms to improve the deal.
When the seller has agreed to ship and expressed readiness to complete the deal, avoid introducing unrelated technical issues that do not advance price negotiation or terms.
When the seller has already provided a firm discounted price and quantity details, avoid asking questions that do not directly challenge the price or create leverage for a better deal.
When the seller makes a clear counteroffer with a discounted price, you should accept the counteroffer to secure a better deal and finalize the agreement efficiently.

When the seller responds to a bulk purchase offer by lowering the price but still above the buyer's target, you should leverage your willingness to buy multiple items to negotiate closer to your desired price.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer below their initial price, you should accept the offer to finalize the deal and secure better terms.
When the seller agrees to a price but is motivated to sell quickly, you should propose favorable payment or delivery terms to reduce your risk without lowering the price.
When the seller has agreed to a price and terms without concessions, avoid raising unrelated product questions that do not influence the negotiated price or terms.
When the seller has made a reasonable counteroffer and agreed to buyer conditions, avoid accepting immediately without attempting to negotiate further for a better price or terms.
When the seller states an initial price, you should make a clear lower counteroffer to signal strong negotiation intent and encourage the seller to reduce their price.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer close to your target price, you should propose a slightly improved offer to finalize the deal efficiently.
When the seller firmly holds a high minimum price and rejects low offers, you should make incremental concessions to encourage the seller to lower their price slightly.
When the seller makes a counteroffer close to their initial price, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially secure a better deal.
When the seller has stated a firm price but the product has a notable limitation, you should highlight that drawback to justify a lower offer and prompt price reduction.
When the seller maintains a firm price based on product value, you should leverage willingness to accept minor losses or inconveniences to create new price anchors and prompt seller concessions.
When the seller has accepted your final price offer and the negotiation is effectively concluded, avoid making non-negotiation statements that do not advance or improve the deal.
When the seller offers additional items but maintains a high price, you should raise valid concerns about product authenticity to leverage a price reduction.
When the seller indicates a firm but flexible price, you should make a lower offer combined with a concession, such as willingness to wait, to encourage the seller to reduce their price.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer below their initial price, you should accept it to secure a favorable deal and finalize the negotiation efficiently.
When the seller indicates that the item’s specifics affect pricing, you should provide clear, relevant details about the item to encourage a price adjustment.
When the seller has made a price concession but the buyer accepts enthusiastically without further negotiation, avoid signaling eagerness that reduces leverage for additional price reductions.
When the seller has made a price concession and set a meeting time without further negotiation, avoid immediately accepting without attempting to negotiate better terms or confirm flexibility.
When the seller responds to a low counteroffer by lowering their price slightly and adding value, you should use a strategic counteroffer to pressure the seller toward a better overall deal.
When the seller offers a bundled deal with a small price concession, you should propose additional non-monetary flexibility to further reduce the price while maintaining value.
When the seller has already agreed to your proposed price and terms, avoid making additional statements that do not contribute to further negotiation or value creation.
When the seller makes a clear price concession but the buyer accepts without further negotiation, avoid conceding prematurely and losing leverage to push for a better price.
When the seller has made a clear counteroffer and provided meeting details, avoid closing the conversation without attempting further negotiation to secure a better price.
When the seller has confirmed a counteroffer price, avoid immediately accepting without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage for a better deal.
When the seller acknowledges a product flaw but maintains a firm price, you should emphasize specific drawbacks to encourage the seller to lower the price or add value.
When the seller rejects a low cash offer and proposes a trade-in plus cash, avoid increasing your cash offer while adding conditional items that weaken your bargaining position.
When the seller proposes a combined cash and item offer to reach a target price, avoid increasing your cash offer without gaining additional concessions, as it weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller responds positively to a near-counteroffer with added value, you should make a small concession close to their price to quickly secure a favorable deal.
When the seller firmly maintains the original price but offers additional value through accessories, avoid focusing solely on requesting free items without addressing the price directly.
When the seller requests specific product details that affect pricing, avoid simply confirming without negotiating to prevent losing leverage and allowing the seller to raise the price.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer above your initial price, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and secure a better deal.
When the seller reiterates the product's excellent condition and firm pricing, avoid responding with non-substantive greetings that do not advance the negotiation or address price.

When the seller confirms the product includes standard and additional accessories without adjusting the price, avoid asking questions that do not directly challenge the price or express willingness to negotiate.
When the seller offers a price reduction contingent on a specific condition, you should accept the counteroffer with the condition to secure a better deal and move the negotiation forward.
When the seller shows interest in a trade-in offer, you should specify the exact details of the item to increase perceived value and improve your chances of lowering the price.
When the seller has already accepted your offer and finalized the deal, avoid sending additional messages that do not contribute to negotiation or leverage.
When the seller maintains a firm price with only a slight concession after the buyer reveals a low budget, avoid revealing your exact cash limit early as it can weaken your negotiating position.
When the seller reiterates the price and highlights included accessories to justify it, avoid asking clarifying questions that allow the seller to strengthen their offer without conceding on price.
When the seller offers a price reduction contingent on a specific condition like pickup, you should accept the condition to secure a better price and demonstrate flexibility in negotiation.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate on price, you should offer a higher price combined with a convenience that reduces the seller's effort to increase acceptance likelihood.
When the seller agrees to a lower price contingent on buyer convenience, you should acknowledge the agreement positively to reinforce the deal and maintain goodwill.
When the seller states a firm initial price, you should directly propose your target price to establish a clear negotiation baseline and assert your position effectively.
When the seller maintains a firm price without engaging further, avoid sending unclear or ambiguous messages that fail to advance your price negotiation effectively.
When the seller maintains a firm initial price but shows willingness to negotiate, you should make a lower offer with a personal reason to encourage a significant price reduction.

When the seller responds to your low offer with a higher counteroffer, you should strengthen your position by adding urgency or convenience, such as immediate pickup, to encourage the seller to lower their price.
When the seller makes a firm counteroffer close to their minimum acceptable price, avoid immediately accepting without attempting to negotiate further or seek additional concessions.
When the seller confirms the inclusion of brand new accessories and additional items, avoid focusing solely on price reduction without first acknowledging the added value provided.
When the seller reiterates their initial high-priced offer without addressing the buyer's acknowledgment, avoid merely acknowledging the offer without introducing negotiation or price discussion.
When the buyer clearly states budget constraints, you should respond by offering lower-priced options to keep the negotiation moving and increase the chance of a sale.
When the seller offers multiple plans with varying features and prices, you should clearly specify your exact needs to prompt the seller to propose a more affordable option that fits your budget.
When the seller offers a lowest fixed-price plan but the buyer still finds it too expensive, you should explore alternative payment models like pre-pay or pay-as-you-go to uncover cheaper options.
When the buyer signals a minimal or highly specific need that implies a lower price threshold, you should ask about their budget to open the door for tailored, cost-sensitive offers.
When the seller offers a price above the buyer's stated budget, you should explicitly narrow your budget range to pressure the seller into proposing an option within your financial limits.
When the seller firmly states that the price is fixed regardless of device ownership, avoid relying on device-related arguments to negotiate a lower price.
When the seller offers a lowest-price plan that meets the buyer's stated budget constraints, you should accept the offer to finalize a deal that secures the best possible price.
When the seller has accepted your offer and confirmed the deal, avoid making additional comments that do not contribute to improving the price or terms.
When the seller states a firm initial price, you should appeal to financial constraints to prompt a price reduction below your initial offer.
When the seller offers a price below their initial asking price, you should accept the offer enthusiastically to finalize a favorable deal without unnecessary further negotiation.
When the seller shows willingness to negotiate and makes a counteroffer, you should make a firm, immediate offer to anchor the price closer to your target.
When the seller makes a reasonable counteroffer and shows willingness to negotiate, you should incrementally increase your offer while expressing your constraints to encourage acceptance.
When the seller has clarified product details and shows willingness to negotiate, you should directly propose your target price to encourage acceptance and move the negotiation forward.
When the seller has made a price concession and included a bonus item, you should request additional value-added items to improve the deal without increasing the price.
When the seller has agreed to a price and included extras, avoid merely confirming terms without attempting to negotiate further or seek additional concessions.
When the seller clearly confirms the agreed price and included extras, avoid unnecessary delays or attempts to renegotiate that may jeopardize closing the deal.
When the seller indicates the buyer's initial offer is too low and asks for more details, you should adjust your offer upward within your target range to encourage a closer counteroffer.
When the seller makes a clear, reasonable counteroffer close to your target price, you should accept promptly to secure a favorable deal and avoid unnecessary further negotiation.
When the seller confirms the product is flawless and cites a higher market price, you should ask condition-related questions to prompt the seller to justify their price and reveal value information.
When the seller holds firm on an initial price, you should make a specific lower counteroffer to pressure the seller into making a meaningful concession.
When the seller makes a counteroffer above your initial offer, avoid immediately accepting it without attempting further negotiation to maintain leverage and potentially lower the final price.
When the seller clarifies and holds firm on a counteroffer after the buyer's accidental low offer, avoid immediately admitting error as it weakens your negotiation leverage.
When the seller offers a conditional discount based on referrals, avoid failing to explicitly confirm or leverage the referral to secure the agreed price reduction.
When the seller counters with a firm price above your initial offer, you should increase your offer closer to their counter to encourage acceptance and progress the negotiation.
When the seller agrees to a price but introduces additional costs like separate shipping fees, avoid accepting the offer immediately without negotiating or clarifying the total final price.

When the seller has made a counteroffer above your initial price, you should show flexibility by increasing your offer slightly while appealing to personal circumstances to build empathy and encourage concession.
When the seller clearly states their minimum acceptable price, avoid immediately conceding to that price without attempting to negotiate further to maintain leverage.
When the seller maintains a firm price without addressing buyer doubts, avoid making indirect challenges that do not clearly propose a price adjustment or negotiation leverage.
When the seller acknowledges a buyer's specific item detail without changing the price, avoid assuming this information alone will immediately lower the asking price.
When the seller responds positively to your information about your item, you should acknowledge their reaction enthusiastically to build rapport and encourage a price concession.
When the seller has already reduced the price but remains open to negotiation, you should offer additional trade items or value to justify and secure a further price reduction.
When the seller agrees to a lower price after a trade-in proposal, you should promptly accept to finalize the improved terms and secure the negotiated discount.
When the seller shifts the negotiation focus to trade-in value after a buyer lowers their cash offer, avoid reducing your cash offer without reinforcing the value of your trade-in items.
When the seller sets a condition for the deal, you should directly confirm that you meet the condition to strengthen your leverage and secure agreement at your target price.
When the seller has accepted a lower price contingent on a trade, you should confirm your commitment clearly and set a meeting to solidify the agreement and move the negotiation forward.
When the seller firmly states their price and justifies it with product quality, avoid lowering your counteroffer below your initial price as it may weaken your negotiation position.
When the seller reduces the price by offering a simpler product option, you should propose a trade-off like self-pickup to lower the price further without excessive concessions.
When the seller has already accepted a lower price with specific conditions, avoid simply confirming the deal without attempting to negotiate additional benefits or terms.
When the seller expresses flexibility and willingness to negotiate, avoid lowering your initial offer before receiving a counteroffer as it weakens your leverage and signals eagerness to concede.
When the seller shows flexibility and willingness to negotiate price, avoid repeating initial interest without making a new offer or referencing prior negotiation progress.
When the seller firmly states their lowest acceptable price, avoid making only minimal incremental offers that fail to significantly narrow the price gap or increase your leverage.
When the seller firmly states a non-negotiable minimum price including shipping, avoid increasing your offer with additional conditions that do not lower the total price, as it weakens your leverage.
When the seller firmly refuses to lower the price further, you should signal your willingness to walk away to create pressure for the seller to reconsider their position.
